title: Nepal DNA-tests 3,685 samples after devastating flood — Dawn - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal DNA-tests 3,685 samples after devastating flood — Dawn  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, forensic laboratories are conducting DNA testing on thousands of samples to establish the identities of people killed in massive flooding. As Dawn reports, the country's authorities have recovered 1,454 bodies, although about one-third of them are only fragments of remains. Families have been handed over 112 identified bodies.

In Nepal, 5,285 people are missing, including hundreds of foreigners. In China, according to state media, 43 people have died and another 519 are considered missing. Overall, the death toll in the two countries is approaching 1,500, while the number of missing people is nearing 5,800.

Thousands of samples for comparison

The flooding was caused by a wave of icy water and debris that formed after a glacier and rocks collapsed on the Nepal-China border on August 26. Some bodies were carried far downstream by the water, complicating their identification.

Two forensic laboratories in Kathmandu are processing 3,685 samples, including more than 1,300 taken from recovered remains. Mukul Pradhan, chief scientific officer at the National Forensic Science Laboratory, noted that the laboratory usually analyses between 1,000 and 1,500 samples per year, mainly in paternity cases or criminal investigations.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Blood samples are easier to analyse, while examining teeth or bones can take several days. Nepalese authorities have buried more than 1,200 bodies after numbering and marking them so that the remains can be exhumed if a DNA match is established.

Help from international specialists

Nirajan Thapa, head of the biology department at the National Forensic Science Laboratory, explained that one DNA profile from remains is not enough: it must be compared with a sample from a relative. Therefore, specialists must process materials from both unidentified remains and thousands of family members of missing people.

Teams from India, China and South Korea have provided assistance to Nepal. Fingerprint experts from the United States and Singapore have also joined the work. According to Thapa's assessment, with such support, sample matching could begin within a few weeks.

Fifty-three-year-old Rajesh Ram, whose son Suroj Kumar went missing in flooded Betravati, told AFP that he had unsuccessfully searched for his son's body. Some families have already held symbolic cremation ceremonies for those missing.

title: Photographing photogenic Nepal - Nepali Times
description: Photographing photogenic Nepal  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
Ajay Narsingh Rana grew up in Kathmandu’s urban jungle. His father Mohan Narsingh designed postage stamps, using photographs of impeyan pheasants, ghoral, and butterflies to convert them into line drawings on tissue paper and printed on tiny stamps depicting Nepal’s rich biodiversity.

Rana’s uncle was a forester from whom he was inspired to look out for flora and fauna in tiny green pockets still left in the city. Growing up in a household that maintained a closeness to the natural world and images portraying it laid the foundation of what was to become Rana’s lifelong passion: photographing Nepal’s biodiversity.

He took up mountain biking and hit the trekking trails, pedalling deep into the wilderness of the mountains and plains. He always had his camera handy, but says one does not even have to be a technically proficient photographer to take good pictures in Nepal — the country is already so photogenic.

While international photographers concentrated on the megafauna like tigers and elephants, Rana was fascinated by what his macro lens could capture. He zoomed in on tiny creepy crawlies, discovering their vibrant colours, unique textures, and shapes hard to see with the naked eye.

The Covid lockdown of 2020 and the restrictions on travel allowed him to capture nature in its minutest detail in the small patch of greenery near his home in Kathmandu. As expected it was buzzing with insects, arachnids, worms, butterflies, grasshoppers, of all shapes, sizes and colours.

It was the monsoon six years ago, and there were even the carnivorous larvae of fireflies crawling about devouring snails in the undergrowth. An open space that many would not even give a second glance to as they drove past was a treasure trove of life.

“They were hopping, buzzing, fluttering, and zooming around all over, you just had to look,” he recalls. “Human beings are evolved into thinking that insects are harmful and zap them if they get the chance, but they are vital to the ecosystem.”

He googled the images to identify and classify the insect pictures, and started posting the images on his website, sharing them on social media to spread his knowledge, get people excited about small living things. The site then grew into a wider platform to celebrate Nepal’s rich biodiversity in pictures.

It is no surprise that Ajaya Narsingh Rana’s self-published new book, The Wild Wonders of Nepal, starts with the smallest critters, the rich birdlife, to charismatic large mammals of Nepal, photographed using macro to tele lens. The book is a visual feast of nature at its most abundant, rich and wild — a diversity that is possible because of the incredible altitude and climate variation of the country.

Rana’s passion for nature and the need to protect it shows through in every photograph, caption, and explanatory text. He has taken meticulous pains to get the reproduction of the photographs exactly right. And the result is a picture-perfect book.

The Wild Wonders of Nepal, is being launched on 2 October, and is sprinkled with quotes from international environmentalists, and this one by the American scientist Jonas Salk seems truest to the message Rana tries to convey: ‘If all the insects were to disappear from the Earth within 50 years, all life on Earth would end. If all human beings disappeared from Earth within 50 years, all life on Earth would flourish.’

The Wild Wonders of Nepal

Ajay Narsingh Rana

title: Nepal to Begin Draining Four Dangerous Glacial Lakes — Reuters - UA.NEWS
description: Nepal to Begin Draining Four Dangerous Glacial Lakes — Reuters  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
Nepal is launching a six-year, $50 million project aimed at lowering the water levels of four glacial lakes in the Himalayas. The goal is to reduce the risk of natural dams bursting and large-scale flooding.

The decision was made following a deadly disaster in August caused by a glacier collapse, landslides, and flash floods. According to authorities, more than 1,400 people were killed, and over 5,000 are still missing.

The work will cover Lakes Tulagi, Lower Barun, Lumding Tso, and Hongu II, located at altitudes ranging from 4,050 to 5,483 meters. The plan is to divert the water in a controlled manner through special channels to neighboring rivers.

The project involves installing sensors, flood forecasting and early warning systems, as well as preparing communities living downstream. Major construction will begin after detailed studies and may take up to six years.

Funding in the amount of $50 million will be provided by the Green Climate Fund, UNDP, and the Government of Nepal. The country has previously lowered the water levels of the hazardous glacial lakes Tso Rolpa and Imja.

Source: Reuters

title: Nepal Telecom suffers $5.8m damage from extreme floods - Developing Telecoms
description: Nepal Telecom suffers $5.8m damage from extreme floods  Developing Telecoms
publisher.title: Developing Telecoms
full_article:
State-owned operator Nepal Telecom suffered around NPR88 million (US$5.8 million) in damage after extreme flooding affected parts of South and Southeast Asia.

The Nepali government said the floods damaged Nepal Telecom's mobile and backbone transmission networks in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts, where more than 1,400 people were killed and 5,000 were reported missing.

Economic Times reported, Information and Communications Minister Bikram Timilsina told the House of Representatives that 83 of Nepal Telecom's 120 sites were affected, with around 70% of the operator's sites taken offline.

Three sites were completely destroyed, while service has been restored at the remaining affected sites. The restored sites are supporting customers in areas around the damaged towers.

Timilsina said 37.9km of Nepal Telecom's 65.3km fibre network in the affected districts had been damaged, with 27.4km already repaired.

Three optical line terminals in Rasuwa and Nuwakot were also completely destroyed.

title: Nepal disaster highlights risks for NZ mountains - Phys.org
description: Nepal disaster highlights risks for NZ mountains  Phys.org
publisher.title: Phys.org
full_article:
Credit: Unsplash/CC0 Public Domain

Te Whare Wānanga o Waitaha | University of Canterbury (UC) School of Earth and Environment senior lecturer Dr. Robinson was part of an international research team investigating the Aug. 26 disaster, when a massive rock and ice avalanche in the Himalaya rapidly transformed into a devastating debris flood.

The World Weather Attribution study brought together specialists in landslides, glaciology, climate change, flooding, data science and risk management to understand how such an extreme and complex event occurred.

The study, "Rapid warming in the Himalaya exacerbates geohazard cascades beyond adaptation limits," was published by World Weather Attribution on Sept. 17.

Robinson says no single factor explains the disaster.

"When we combine the role of the earthquake in 2015 with longer-term trends of warming temperatures, the loss of glacial ice and permafrost, and changing snow and rainfall, it's clear that a multitude of factors came together to cause this event."

The study found human-induced climate change has significantly increased temperatures around the site and across the wider Himalaya. Near the collapse site, July and August temperatures are now about 1.5°C warmer and annual temperatures about 1.9°C warmer because of human influence on the climate.

Robinson's contribution focused on whether Nepal's devastating magnitude 7.8 earthquake in 2015 played a role and how this combined with climate-driven changes.

"We knew the earthquake had caused substantial damage in this area and triggered a catastrophic fatal landslide on the other side of the mountain," he says.

"Since then, the number of landslides in this region has increased, particularly at high elevations. That suggests the earthquake damaged and weakened the rock, making these large collapses more likely even years after the event."

Robinson says the conditions that contributed to the Nepal disaster are not unique to the Himalaya.

"We find many of the same conditions here in Aotearoa New Zealand. Our climate is warming, our glaciers are receding rapidly, and at higher elevations we are seeing less snow and more rain."

While the Southern Alps have not experienced a major earthquake recently, there is a 75% chance of a major Alpine Fault earthquake in the next 50 years, Robinson says.

"We shouldn't be surprised to see events like this in the Southern Alps in the future," Robinson says.

"Fortunately, they are highly unlikely to be anywhere near the size we saw in Nepal, and we have far fewer people living in our mountains.

"But as tourism grows, particularly in places like Aoraki Mount Cook National Park, we are likely to see more people spending time in mountain environments where these events can happen."

Robinson says the disaster also demonstrates the limits of climate adaptation and the need to reverse climate change.

"No level of adaptation could have prevented or minimized the losses Nepal has seen. While climate adaptation is important, it cannot be our sole focus.

"We need to continue addressing climate change at the source and limit warming by reducing carbon and other greenhouse gas emissions, alongside adaptation."

title: Nepal suspends search after 16 swept away by avalanche - The Indian Panorama
description: Nepal suspends search after 16 swept away by avalanche  The Indian Panorama
publisher.title: The Indian Panorama
full_article:
KATHMANDU (TIP): Dire weather has forced Nepal to suspend search operations after a Himalayan avalanche caused what is feared to be the worst expedition disaster in over a decade, the National Mountain Guide Association said.

Since the avalanche swept through the base camp of the 7,126-metre (23,345-foot) Himlung peak early on Sunday, four bodies have been recovered while 12 people remain missing.

“The conditions are very challenging,” said Tul Singh Gurung, president of the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association. “The search has been paused”.

The 12 missing people are all Nepali workers preparing for later expeditions on Himlung, near the Chinese border, a popular destination for mountaineers looking to begin climbing 7,000-metre peaks.

Rescue team leader Mingma G Sherpa said he had little hope of finding the missing alive.

“Looking at the bodies recovered, it would be impossible for the rest to survive,” he told AFP. “The scale of the avalanche is massive, we can go back when the snow melts a bit.”

The team of eight mountain guides had reached the base camp on Sunday evening to begin the search, digging through more than four metres (14 feet) of snow.

Tents were buried under deep snow.

The bodies of two mountain guides were recovered on Sunday, and those of two kitchen staff were pulled out earlier this week.

Nepal’s worst mountaineering disasters in recent years occurred in 2014, when an avalanche killed 16 people on Everest, and in 2015, when an earthquake killed 18 people, also on Everest.

Nepal is still searching for bodies from devastating floods sparked by a mountain glacial collapse on August 26 that killed more than 1,400 people and left over 6,000 missing.

Heavy rain since Thursday has triggered other floods and landslides, killing at least 21 people, according to the national disaster agency.

Home to eight of the world’s 14 highest peaks, Nepal relies heavily on mountaineering and trekking tourism.

title: Tennis in Nepal: How the Sport Is Building a Stronger Presence - World Tennis Magazine

Tennis does not yet command the mass audience that cricket enjoys in Nepal, but its footprint is becoming much easier to see. Kathmandu regularly hosts international junior competition, Nepali players are appearing in events abroad, and youth programmes are connecting the country to the wider Asian tennis pathway. Rather than one dramatic breakthrough, tennis in Nepal is developing through tournaments, individual players, coaching and a gradually expanding audience.

Nepal’s Place on the International Tennis Calendar

One of the clearest signs of progress is Nepal’s presence in International Tennis Federation competition. Kathmandu hosted two J60 junior tournaments in early 2026, giving young players the chance to compete for ranking points on home courts. Nepal also hosted South Asian qualifying for the ITF Asia 12 & Under Team Competition in Lalitpur in April, bringing junior teams from across the region together and giving local players valuable international match experience.

For fans, international tennis is also one of the easiest sports to follow statistically. A match can be broken down through rankings, recent results, surface, head-to-head history and tournament draws. Betting markets add another layer of numbers, but odds should be treated as market prices rather than predictions. Someone using a best betting app to compare tennis markets should still check the draw, playing surface, recent workload and player news before interpreting a line.

Players Give Nepali Tennis a Visible International Story

Individual players matter enormously in a developing tennis scene because they give younger athletes a pathway they can actually see. Abhishek Bastola has represented Nepal internationally, competed in the Davis Cup and continued playing events abroad in 2026. Fans following a tournament through a MelBet betting app or another live-score service can use the same basic information that matters to tennis analysis everywhere: current form, opponent level, surface and recent match volume.

Junior players are also giving Nepal more visibility around Asia. In 2026, Nepali juniors competed in ITF pathways and international events outside the country. Shivali Gurung, for example, reached the girls’ doubles title at the J60 Colombo event in September. Results like these are important because junior tennis is where ranking experience, travel routines and exposure to different playing styles begin to accumulate.

Youth Tennis Is the Foundation of Long-Term Growth

Tennis development starts well before a player reaches the Davis Cup or the professional circuit. Nepal’s recent hosting of junior international events shows why a local pathway matters: young athletes need regular matches, coaching, competitive courts and opportunities to face players from other countries.

Junior tournaments: ITF events in Kathmandu allow Nepali players to gain international experience without every competition requiring overseas travel.

Regional competition: South Asian qualifying events expose young players to opponents from neighbouring tennis systems.

Coaching and practice: Consistent technical training is especially important in a sport where movement, serve mechanics and point construction develop over years.

International pathways: Strong junior results can lead toward higher-level ITF events, college opportunities and eventually professional competition.

This structure does more than produce elite players. Regular junior competition gives families, coaches and local clubs a reason to stay involved, while international events create measurable goals for developing athletes. For Nepal, the challenge is not simply discovering one exceptional player but making the route from beginner to competitive tennis more consistent.

Recent Tennis Highlights in Nepal

Nepal’s 2026 tennis calendar offered several useful signs of activity. Kathmandu hosted back-to-back J60 junior tournaments from late January into early February, while Lalitpur staged the South Asian qualifying event for the ITF Asia 12 & Under Team Competition in April. These events put Nepali courts directly into the regional development system rather than leaving local players dependent only on domestic competition.

At the senior level, Abhishek Bastola remained one of the most visible Nepali players internationally in 2026. He competed abroad on professional and UTR circuits while preparing for major regional competition. His experience also highlights one of the difficulties facing tennis in Nepal: international travel, coaching, equipment and tournament entry create costs that can be much harder to absorb in an individual sport than in a centrally funded team programme.

Courts, Phones and Streams: How Fans Follow Tennis

Tennis is well suited to digital viewing because matches generate a constant stream of useful information. Fans can move between live scores, draws, rankings, highlights and short match clips without needing to watch every point. Grand Slam events and major ATP and WTA tournaments also give Nepali viewers a global entry point into the sport, while local and regional competitions make that interest more relevant at home.

Social media can help close the visibility gap between major international stars and Nepali players. Tournament results, training clips and junior achievements can circulate quickly, giving athletes exposure even when traditional television coverage is limited. For a smaller tennis market, that digital layer is particularly important because it keeps the sport visible between the relatively few major events held in Nepal.

Where Tennis in Nepal Can Go Next

The future of Nepali tennis depends less on a sudden popularity boom than on continuity. Hosting ITF junior tournaments, strengthening coaching, maintaining usable courts and helping talented players compete internationally can gradually deepen the sport’s base. Nepal already has an official national association within the international tennis structure and has shown that it can host regional and junior events. If those opportunities become more regular, tennis can build a stronger identity alongside Nepal’s larger sports. The most useful signs will be practical ones: more juniors playing ranked events, more Nepali athletes travelling competitively, better access to coaching and a calendar that gives players meaningful matches throughout the year.

description: Nepal Floods: Why Big Dams Can Deepen Disaster  Frontline Magazine

full_article:
The recent floods in Nepal killed over 1,400 people and destroyed thousands of homes. According to Daanish Mustafa, professor of critical geography at King’s College London, linking climate change to the disaster does nothing to shift the goal away from adapting meaningfully. He says the root of the crisis lies in the neocolonial mindset that infuses importance and pride to high-impact projects for grand outcomes and to commercial activities that cater to certain entrenched interests. Mustafa has spent much of his career researching water, hazards, and the relationship between landscapes and human development in South Asia. Edited excerpts: What are your thoughts on the recent floods in Nepal? How much damage could have been avoided through better planning, infrastructure and disaster preparedness? The Nepal flood happened in a very small catchment. It was basically a glacial slip that fell into a moraine, and then there was a wall of water that came down. Most people don’t remember the Chong Kumdan flood of 1929. That happened in the Shyok valley, in the Karakoram. And that flood caused the railway bridge in Attock to be swept away from a 15-20 metre-high wave, a thousand kilometres down from where the GLOF [glacial lake outburst flood] had happened. In the Karakoram, you end up having glaciers that are 100 times bigger than the Eastern Himalayan glaciers, and you have rivers that are 100 times bigger than the Eastern Himalayan rivers. Then, you’re building dams—the tallest dam in the world, 750 feet [229 m] high, the Diamer-Bhasha is being built. It’s 1,000 times bigger than any hydroelectric projects that you had in Nepal. So imagine a scenario of a wall like that coming down, taking out an 892-foot [272 m] high dam. Then there’s a Dasu dam downstream of it; it’ll take that out. Then it’ll take the Tarbela out. Then, it’ll take every piece of infrastructure out because every time you breach a structure, you further amplify the wave. There’s a nuclear reactor in Chashma, right by the river Indus, about 200-300 km downstream of Attock. If that goes, Pakistan will be uninhabitable for the next 50,000 years. Pakistan, Indian Punjab, and Kashmir. That’s the level of catastrophic scenario we are looking at. Also Read | Nepal floods: What went wrong and what’s next? What is changing in South Asia’s water systems? Are we seeing changes in the intensity, timing, or distribution of rainfall, riverflow, snow and glacial melt, also given climate change? Did the Nepal disaster happen because of climate change? Maybe it did, maybe it did not. But it doesn’t matter because the Karakoram and the Hindu Kush region is one of the most dynamic regions in the world: it is seismically active, there are earthquakes every day. There’s a plate going down which doesn’t care if there is climate change or not. Ice, glaciers, cryosphere: it’s a dynamic system. Glaciers move. Glaciers recede. Glaciers grow. Glaciers die out. Hydrologically, it’s the most dynamic mountain range in the world. You can take white man’s science and pretend that we control it, pretend that we know it, pretend that we can predict it. Your pretence has fallen apart. It never worked. The fact is that what you’re trying to do in the high Himalaya is just something that is foolhardy to try. There’s a reason that with the same neural density, with the same intellectual capacity, for thousands of years, South Asian societies said “We’re not going to mess with that stuff.” And in the last 150 years, the British came and they said, “We’re going to show you Brown people how our white science can do things that you never thought should be done.” And you’re reaping the consequences. When you start thinking about decolonising water, you’re talking about precisely that. The Christian missionaries always took science with them. They tried to undermine all the mythologies and the local knowledge of glaciers and mountains. I think that these tropes of climate change: how do you tell the difference? There are so many more people living in the flat plains. We have so much of a richer gauge network now to actually measure those things. The exposed populations are so much greater. Groundwater extraction is so much more. The extractivism is so much more intense. How do I separate out the climate signal from the political economy of why people are living where they are living? You can try, but to what effect? So what will that do? One of the political signals is that, “It’s not our fault.” The real estate people get off the hook and chase away poor people from their lands, from their livelihoods, and build these ghastly projects that will further constrict the channels and therefore further accentuate the flood peaks. A vehicle rides along the Nepal-China Highway near the Bhote Koshi River at Syabrubesi in Nepal's Rasuwa district on September 29, 2026, in the aftermath of the August 26 flash flood. | Photo Credit: PRAKASH MATHEMA/AFP How can large infrastructure in mountain regions amplify the consequences of floods, landslides and glacial hazards? How does a large dam accentuate the damage? In a couple of ways. The worst case scenario is that very few dams in the world—depending upon the size of the GLOF and what have you—can withstand the GLOF that we are doing. You’ve breached a lake, the storage of water broke and came right down. And then you come across another lake that you’ve built. And it is going to break that. When a boulder the size of two houses hits a dam, it’s going to go. And when it goes, you have created another GLOF. So that’s the obvious one way in which it makes things worse. The other one is that the lower dams like Mangla, Tarbela, and Bhakra Nangal, and others, what you do is you hold back a lot of silt within those dams. You also eliminate flood pulses. All rivers have a flood pulse. It’s monsoon season; the river’s going to flood; it is going to spread out on to the flood plain. What we have done is we have engineered a way to moderate floods with the dams and diversions. [By doing so we have] exchanged high-frequency, low-intensity events for low-frequency, high-intensity events. Every dam has a safe design capacity that it can take. The whole protocol for flood management is that infrastructure must not be lost. When a barrage’s safe design capacity is exceeded, they breach the right bank of the river and flood out the surrounding lands in order to protect the infrastructure, because if you don’t, then you lose the infrastructure. In the case of India, once the safe capacity of the dam is exceeded, that’s when you open all the gates. When Satluj and Ravi both open their gates, you get catastrophic damage. You just did in 2025. So when you build infrastructure, your priority is to protect the infrastructure. And you can never build an infrastructure which is completely flood-proof. You can’t, it’s just not possible. In the case of Pakistan, it is a standard operating procedure that all reservoirs should be as full as possible by August 20. In the past, we have seen that the flood peaks have happened in September, so when a flood peak comes down, it comes across a full reservoir, then if you don’t open the reservoir, you lose the reservoir. If you open up the reservoir, catastrophic damage happens downstream of it. Also, when you hold back the silt, what you’re doing is reducing channel capacity. For 5 to 10 years, you’ve not allowed floods to happen. What used to be a medium flood becomes a high flood, what becomes a high flood becomes a very high flood, and a very high flood becomes a catastrophic flood. That’s the bargain you have made with infrastructure. Does this trade-off come every time one builds a dam? Of course. Certainly, in South Asia. Our rivers drain the youngest mountains in the world. Hence, they carry the largest silt load in the world. So, large-dam building technology was fundamentally invented in Europe and North America. If you compare the Colorado River, which is the size of a minor tributary of the Ganges, and say, “They built a dam; why don’t we build a dam like that?” Or the Murray-Darling basin, if you’ve ever seen the Murray-Darling basin in Australia, you will be like, “You’re calling this a river?” We won’t even call it a stream in India. When you have the size of the kind of rivers that you have in South Asia, and when you consider the silt loads, they didn’t even understand what silt loads meant in the 1950s and 1960s when they were building these dams. Now we do. But all the textbooks in Indian and Pakistani engineering departments are written by dead white people who were studying these streams in North America and Europe, which has got nothing to do with us. The problems that we are seeing today are very much a function of the colonial mindset with colonial education. Lower dams, like the Bhakra-Nangal dam, hold back a lot of silt and eliminate flood pulses. | Photo Credit: Mrinal Pal/Getty Images What can governments do to make people better informed and better prepared, particularly at the local level? In the first instance, early warnings. But your early warning is your legacy colonial scientific system. Its articulation is in a language that no one understands. It makes them happy because they’ve given you an objective reality but it does nothing. First of all, make it vernacular. It has to be in terms that are understandable. India is gigantic. There’s local meteorology there. So for that, what you need to have is a denser network of registrations, involving more people in citizen meteorology. I’ve always made the case for Pakistan’s meteorological department—why can’t you have a $10 weather station on top of every government school in Pakistan? Children collect data so they understand the data. If people do it, they understand and believe it. In the context of Pakistan, what works in Balochistan doesn’t work in Punjab, what works in Punjab is not good for Gilgit-Baltistan. So it is context specific. Is the perception that environmental and construction regulations are weaker in the Global South than in the advanced countries a fair assessment? To what extent can regulatory failures turn natural hazards into large disasters? Is there no corruption in the Global North? Having lived in the Global North, I don’t see much of a difference. They just do it in English. How can local communities be involved in planning and in designing systems to predict and to prepare for these catastrophic events? Let me flip the question on its head. There’s a person sitting in Roorkee or in Kolkata or in Delhi planning a massive canal project in Gujarat. Goes there for four to five days, takes pictures, checks it out. Comes back, designs the whole thing. What stupefies me is that person is involved, but the person living there is not. The absurdity of it is that someone who has never [set] foot in a particular place has the right [to plan], and the people who are actually living there [and have] spent their whole lives there—their Gods are there, their mythologies, their spirituality, their identity, everything is there—do not. So the question itself is the answer in a manner of speaking. The biggest issue with rivers and flooding in the Indus basin is drainage. Once the water comes, you have to drain it. Which way does the drainage go? No engineer in the Pakistani irrigation department can tell you which way the drainage goes. The local people know. Even a child can tell you, “The water goes that way.” But that’s the person you don’t want to shake hands with. That’s the person you don’t want to listen to. So, to my mind, “how can the local community be involved” is a question that needs reflection. What if one were to ask, “How can engineers be involved?” That sounds like a more difficult question except that it’s the easiest one to answer. People walk on the dry riverbed of the Indus River in Hyderabad, Pakistan, April 24, 2025. | Photo Credit: YASIR RAJPUT/REUTERS How should governments reconcile the economic importance of agriculture and industry with the need for long-term water security? The largest exporter of embedded water in agricultural products in the world is Pakistan. Who benefits from sugarcane production? The exporters do. There’s a certain structure of subsidies that are offered to them. The highest incidence of malnourishment in Pakistan is in the irrigated districts. How can you have the highest level of per-capita malnourishment in the country in the regions which have the highest agricultural production? The answer is right there, because that land and that water is going towards the production of cash crops that benefit certain agro-capitalist interests exporting overseas or domestically. A poor person drawing water from a water well in rural Bengal is not an economic actor. Yet [multinational corporations] taking all that water away, packaging it and selling it to you [and] making millions in the process is an economic activity [and] beneficial for the country. That person’s dysentery, that person’s malnourishment is not a statistic that is of interest. Eight hundred million people in India depend upon the Indian government for ration for their food security. But that does not feature in the conversations. This is outrageous. So, I think if you buy into the parameters of a conversation or buy into the assumptions of the conversation, it takes you only in one direction—when you’re talking about economic growth and development and all the rest of it. If you talk about a different framework, you can change the parameters of the conversation. In many cities, some people have abundant access to water while others travel long distances for basic needs. What does a fair system of water allocation look like? There are children dying of renal failure in Karachi—80 per cent of the population of Karachi is water insecure. It turns out that there are about 25 golf courses in Karachi; one golf course takes up enough water for about 22,000 households. Half a kilometre from the [DHA Golf Club] is a child dying of renal failure because they are drinking saline water. That’s the water story of South Asia and in that story is everything that’s wrong with the development model. How should governments approach developments in wetlands, floodplains, mountain regions, and other landscapes? Every square centimetre of this planet is ecologically sensitive. There is some ecological cost that you have to bear. Ultimately, instead of getting into the idiom of ecology, why don’t we get into the idiom of human dignity or the idiom of livelihoods where there is clean drinking water in the spring? When you’re talking about a nice, clean forest, when you’re talking about healthy fisheries in a stream, you’re talking about the food security of the people who depend on the stream. An equitable, just society will have a robust ecology because that’s how people gain their livelihood, their food security, their cultural belonging, their dignity. So why worry about ecology, why not worry about dignity? When you start talking in those terms, then a different conversation emerges which takes everyone along. The closed gates of the Salal Dam on the Chenab river after the suspension of the Indus Waters Treaty, in Reasi district, Jammu and Kashmir, May 5, 2025. | Photo Credit: PTI How should governments decide between competing claims on water from households, agriculture, industry and emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence? I’m very sceptical of AI. They have very good uses in, say, engineering, medicine, in specific niche kinds of situations, and in the military. But if you are devoting stupefying amounts of water and land, taking it away from its other uses, urgent uses, you make funny cartoons and fake pictures and made-up term papers—no comedy or tragedy in the world could capture the sheer stupidity of it all. The second thing is: isn’t it funny that 70 per cent of the new energy demand in the United States is coming from data centres and AI? Do you really want to devote all of those resources to an algorithm? To what effect? Who is it benefiting? The elites don’t care for our people. Let not a man from Silicon Valley come over there, take away your land, take away your water, and suck up all the energy. That could be put to other uses. My view is: how do you decide? Don’t go there. Because this is all going to go bust. AI cannot work. Certainly not with the energy cost, let alone the water cost. Not one company will tell you how much energy goes into it. So once you understand it, it’s a fraud, don’t do it. Also Read | The human cost of conservation As we see water stress and extreme hydrological events, how important will transboundary cooperation become? It is essential. For example, I have been telling everyone in Pakistan that Pakistan should thank [Prime Minister Narendra] Modi for pulling out of the Indus Waters Treaty. When the Indus Waters Treaty was signed, in 1960, they did not understand silt. They did not understand surface and groundwater dynamics. The day we destabilise the capitalist model of agriculture, the sheer absurdity of fighting over water will become apparent. Because water is going to flow in that direction, it’s going to flow downhill no matter what you do. Eighty per cent of the crop-water requirement in Pakistan comes from groundwater, which is also true in Indian Punjab. So, the whole transboundary water conflict is basically an argument between gangsters: who gets to do the worst to the river. My submission to you is that that is a losing proposition. If we change the parameters of the conversation, then you’ll automatically find that the free and flowing river is to the benefit of India as it is to the benefit of Bangladesh. A free and flowing river is as much to the benefit of Nepal as it is to the benefit of India, in Bihar. How that will emerge is when you’re thinking about the lives and livelihoods of people who live by the river, not the fantasies of the engineers and planners in the capital. The problem is with them, the problem is not with the people. title: A Plan B First Ascent: Nepal Landslides Force Veteran Italians to Change Peaks - Explorersweb »
description: A Plan B First Ascent: Nepal Landslides Force Veteran Italians to Change Peaks  Explorersweb »
publisher.title: Explorersweb »
full_article:
It’s become their custom: Nives Meroi and Romano Benet are back in Nepal to attempt a new route or a first ascent of a scarcely visited 6,000m peak. The recent landslides affecting the Manang region have forced them to change their destination, but not their ambitions.

Their original goal was a new route on the south face of 7,134m Tilicho, north of Annapurna. However, landslides caused by heavy rain last weekend have severely affected that region. The Italian couple, who always walk to their base camp, were unable to reach Tatopani, the starting point of the trek. Usually, the town is accessible by road, but now even footpaths are not possible.

“We were told there were 46 landslides along the route, and conditions of the path to base camp [beyond Tatopani] are unknown,” Meroi told ExplorersWeb from Kathmandu.

Benet posted today that they have found an alternative goal, something they can reach on foot rather than by helicopter. Hiking in is part of the expedition for them, and they have no wish to change that.

Plan B: Jugal II

“We’ve decided to explore the Jugal Himal area, recently opened to climbers,” Benet wrote. “Information is scarce, but we’ve decided to attempt unclimbed Jugal II (6,518m).”

The main peaks of the Jugal Himal. Photo: Nepali News Hub

Meroi and Benet, who have both summited all the 8000’ers without supplemental oxygen, have also pioneered several new routes and first ascents. Meroi earned a Piolet d’Or for his climb of Kabru II in the Kangchenjunga region. For Jugal II, Tine Cuder of Slovenia has joined them as a third.

The Jugal Himal is quite close to Kathmandu, just northeast of town on the border with Tibet. It’s reachable by bus with a few days’ trekking, as Paul Ramsden explained when he opened a new route on Jugal Spire with Tim Miller. This climb also earned them a Piolet d’Or.

These peaks have been so rarely visited because until 2023, they were closed to climbing. That spring, Nepal opened Jugal I (6,591m) and Jugal II (6,518m), together with five other peaks in the area.

In spring 2024, veteran Um Hong-gil of South Korea launched a Korean-Nepalese expedition featuring Sherpa celebrities Dawa Yangzum and Lakpa Dendi, to unclimbed Jugal I and Jugal II. They successfully summited Jugal I, but not Jugal II, which remains unclimbed, according to The Himalayan Database.

Climbers, circled, on the final ridge of Jugal I. Photo: Korean-Nepalese Friendship Expedition 2024

Annapurna trails closed

Several Nepal trails remain closed due to landslides. Because of contradictory information on social media, trekkers should verify with local outfitters or tourism boards. While the Manaslu Circuit is open, landslides have severely affected the Manang region in general and the Annapurna Circuit in particular. Meanwhile, an avalanche cut the Thorong La, the highest point of the Annapurna trail. Check yesterday’s images, below.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Nepal’s National Trust for Nature Conservation said today that trekking permits for Annapurna are available again, but area trekkers reported that several major landslides have seriously damaged even the Annapurna South Side Base Camp trek. There are power outages and no cell connection.

“As of now [October 1], above Manang, everything is closed,” trekker Krishna Acharya has just posted on Facebook’s Annapurna Circuit Trek group.

The change of plans of even this hardcore Italian team suggests that the area is not yet suitable for trekking.

title: Germany Returns Over 800 Historic Nepali Documents Dating Back to 13th Century - INDIA New England News
description: Germany Returns Over 800 Historic Nepali Documents Dating Back to 13th Century  INDIA New England News
publisher.title: INDIA New England News
full_article:
Kathmandu – More than 800 historical documents, including manuscripts dating back to the 13th century, have been returned to Nepal from Germany, marking a significant recovery of the country’s cultural and historical heritage.

The collection, which includes ancient palm-leaf manuscripts, royal decrees, court orders, legal records, Sanskrit texts and historical travel accounts, was formally handed over to the National Archives of Nepal on Friday, according to the country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The documents were previously held in the private collection of the late Joseph Peter Rindfleisch. His son, Walter Rindfleisch, transferred the collection to Professor Axel Michaels of the Heidelberg Academy of Sciences and Humanities, who coordinated its return to Nepal.

Michaels, along with researchers Manik Bajracharya and Rajan Khatiwada, handed over the documents to Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal during a ceremony in Kathmandu.

According to the Foreign Ministry, the collection contains materials gathered from Nepal between the 1780s and the 1990s, providing valuable insights into the country’s political, legal, intellectual and cultural history.

The collection includes 465 palm-leaf manuscripts from the Malla period, including royal decrees bearing red seals, and 312 legal decrees and royal documents from the Shah and Rana periods. It also contains 18 manuscripts and travel diaries from the offices of Rana prime ministers and 11 manuscripts covering various subjects.

Some of the palm-leaf manuscripts are among Nepal’s oldest surviving historical documents.

Speaking at the handover ceremony, Khanal described the return as an important step toward restoring Nepal’s cultural rights and ownership of its historical heritage.

“Our art, literature, traditions and sacred scriptures are not merely physical remnants; they are the living soul of our civilisation. They carry centuries of philosophical thought, political governance, legal knowledge and spiritual life,” he said.

Khanal also acknowledged Joseph Peter Rindfleisch’s wish to return the documents to Nepal and praised Michaels and his research team for their work in identifying, preserving and facilitating the repatriation of the materials.

Before their return, the documents were preserved and cataloged by the Heidelberg University Library and the Heidelberg Academy of Sciences and Humanities.

The repatriation was coordinated through a partnership involving Nepal’s Embassy in Germany, Heidelberg University, the Heidelberg Academy of Sciences and Humanities, the Saraf Foundation and Nepal’s National Archives.

Khanal noted that Nepal and Germany are both parties to the 1970 UNESCO Convention, which seeks to prevent the illegal import, export and transfer of cultural property.

He said the handover demonstrated the two countries’ commitment to protecting cultural heritage and expressed appreciation for the support provided by the German government, the German Embassy in Kathmandu and Heidelberg University.

“Today’s handover is an important example of our shared international commitment,” Khanal said. (Source: IANS)

full_article:
KATHMANDU — Nepal will kick off a high-stakes effort this fiscal year to drain four glacial lakes perched high in the mountains, as it scrambles to ⁠reduce flood risks, officials said, after a recent disaster that killed more than 1,400.

Rescuers are still searching for more than 5,000 people missing in the border region with China after August’s glacier collapse unleashed landslides and a flash flood that tore through valleys.

“Our aim is to lower the risk of the lakes breaching their natural dams and reduce the risk of downstream floods,” said Subash Tuladhar, an expert with a government research centre tasked ⁠with overseeing the new project.

Canals will drain water into nearby ​rivers ⁠in a regulated way, he said, adding that workers faced health risks as a result of the lengthy periods of high-altitude work required, in addition to the dangers of sudden flooding.

Nepali Army personnel carry bodies of victims on Aug. 28. Prabin Ranabhat / AFP via Getty

Design work and detailed studies targeting the ⁠central and eastern lakes of Thulagi, Lower Barun, Lumding Tsho and Hongu II, will begin in the fiscal year that ​runs until ⁠mid-July 2027, authorities said.

The lakes, at heights ranging from ‌4,050 m to 5,483 m (13,280 ft to 18,000 ft), rank among Nepal’s most potentially dangerous, the United Nations Development Programme and the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) said in a 2020 report.

Nepal had the skills and experience required for ‌the $50-million project to be funded by the Green Climate Fund, the UNDP and ‌the government, added Tuladhar, of Nepal’s Centre for Hydrology and Water Resources Research.

Draining project could take six years

The work of draining “through gated structures” will start after a detailed study, and could take up to six years to complete, said Sanjeeb Baral, the Centre’s executive director.

It will encompass installation of sensors, a ⁠flood forecasting and warning system, and efforts to build downstream resilience and prepare communities for the risks.

In similar previous efforts, Nepal lowered by 3 m (10 ft) the level of the central Himalayan glacial lake of Tsho Rolpa in 2000, and that of Imja in the vicinity of Mount Everest, the world’s tallest peak, 10 years ago.

The Rasuwagadhi border post on the China-Nepal border before and after the flooding. Satellite image ©2026 Vantor

Urgency after recent floods

Nepal’s disaster served as a warning to the world, Prime Minister Balendra Shah, 36, told the United Nations in an impassioned speech last month that blamed climate change despite his country’s negligible emissions.

Retreating glaciers, unstable mountain slopes and increasingly unpredictable rivers showed Nepal was paying a heavy price, he ‌added.

Nepal, which has reported about 26 Glacial Lake Outburst Flood events in the past four decades, loses ​more than 300 lives and property worth millions of dollars to extreme climate events annually on average.
